catalog_quote: Secondly, not only is the final mora excluded for the stress assignment determination, but in Kangri, all inflectional morphology is excluded as well. As argued below, stress assignment is done in the lexicon and is always assigned exclusively within the stem of the word (i.e. word root plus any derivational affixes). Inflectional affixes, regardless of syllable shape, are never stressed. Given these constraints, the assignment of stress in Kangri can be stated by the following rules: • Looking only at the syllables in the stem of the word, • factoring in extrametricality, • the heaviest, • or right-most heavy syllable is stressed. • If all syllables are LIGHT, then the first syllable is stressed. ... 4.3.1 Stress the Heaviest Syllable in the Stem. new_statements.rule_in_words: Within the stem only (root + derivational affixes; inflectional suffixes invisible), with the word-final mora extrametrical and syllables classed light (CV with ɪ ʊ ə) / heavy (CVV, CVC) / superheavy (CVVC, CVCC): stress the heaviest syllable; among equally heavy syllables stress the right-most heavy one; if all stem syllables are light, stress the first syllable. Unbounded (no window). Eaton classes it as 'fixed' in Hayes's sense (predictable, non-phonemic). Tone (high or contour from underlying /ɦ/) is realized on the stressed syllable, so pitch is not a dependable stress correlate.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not discussed; only primary word stress is described (no mention of secondary stress found in the dissertation).
new_statements.exceptions: Inflectional affixes are never stressed even when they contain bimoraic vowels (sec. 4.3.5); final-mora extrametricality needed for words like [bə.'ɾoo.bəɾ], ['də̌.ɾəm] (Table 4-5); footnote 31 (p. 56): author's opinion that when all syllables have equal weight the word may effectively have no primary stress and the initial stress observed in all-light words may be a citation-form elicitation effect; causative/derivational suffixes count as stem and can bear stress.
new_statements.domain_note: Lexical word stress assigned in the lexicon over the stem domain; data are elicited citation forms from Kangri as spoken in and around Palampur (Kangra district). Author notes no instrumental duration measurements were made.
new_statements.identity_note: Eaton 2008 describes Kangri as spoken in and around Palampur, Kangra district, Himachal Pradesh (glottocode kang1280, ISO xnr); he treats it as a dialect of (Western) Pahari and compares it with Hindi, Punjabi and Dogri. No sub-dialect glottocode needed.

sources.locator: Ch. 4 'Stress', sec. 4.3 'Stress Assignment in Kangri', pp. 52-53 (rule list); typology statement sec. 4.1, p. 49; sub-rules 4.3.1-4.3.5, pp. 53-67
sources.note: Whole Chapter 4 'Stress' (pp. 48-67): stress is fixed (predictable), weight-sensitive and unbounded within the stem; final mora extrametrical; heaviest / right-most heavy stem syllable stressed; if all stem syllables light, first syllable stressed; inflectional affixes never stressed; tone (from /ɦ/) docks on the stressed syllable, so pitch is not a reliable stress cue; fn. 31 (p. 56) opines that words with all-equal-weight syllables may effectively lack primary stress and that initial stress in such citation forms may be an elicitation effect.
